consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge: covenant is a solemn, binding relationship divinely initiated by God with His people, marked by promise, blood ratification, and signs, structuring redemptive history through the successive biblical covenants and culminating in the new covenant in Christ's blood written on the heart. Disagreements listed (covenant theology vs. dispensationalism, marital imagery, ANE treaty form, testament reading) concern architecture and continuity, not the core identification.
book_summary: The book defines covenant as the binding WORD by which a covenant head establishes and governs a relationship through law, promises, and judgments. Parties entering a covenant come under its head and his terms rather than negotiating as autonomous equals. It stresses that God expressly identifies the Ten Commandments as His covenant — something spoken, commanded, written, entered, cut in blood, kept or broken, and renewed by writing the law on the heart. Its common-view note rejects the 'contract negotiated between parties' framing for obscuring the covenant head.
consensus_core_identification: Covenant = a divinely initiated, binding RELATIONSHIP of promise and faithfulness between God and His people, sealed in blood and fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ.
book_core_identification: Covenant = the binding governing WORD (law, promises, judgments) supplied by a covenant head, under which those who enter the covenant come; the relationship is established and governed by that word, with the Ten Commandments expressly called God's covenant.
boundary_disagreement: The book relocates the referent's center of gravity from the relationship itself to the head's governing word that constitutes it (Deut 4:13: the covenant IS the ten commandments). It excludes the 'contract/agreement between negotiating parties' framing that appears in the consensus as a common alternative (treaty/contract readings in Responses A–D), and it admits head-governed human covenants (2 Kgs 11:17, Jehoiada's covenant between king and people) into the same category, which the consensus's God-people framing does not foreground. Cases reclassified: the covenant sign/relationship complex is re-identified as instances of a spoken/written word being entered, kept, broken, and renewed.
material_contradiction: No strict contradiction. The consensus already holds that covenants are divinely initiated rather than negotiated (e.g., Response D's note that God alone passes between the pieces), so the book's anti-contract polemic sharpens rather than overturns the consensus. Saying the covenant is the head's binding word that establishes the relationship does not deny that a binding relationship results; it changes what the term itself names.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus's general referent — God's binding, blood-ratified, divinely imposed arrangement with His people, renewed by writing the law on the heart (Jer 31; Heb 8), which both sides treat as central. But it materially changes the precision and boundary: (1) covenant is identified with the governing word/law itself rather than the relationship it creates; (2) an explicit 'covenant head' structure is made definitional; (3) the bilateral contract/treaty framing, treated by the consensus as a common legitimate alternative, is expressly rejected as an error; (4) human covenants under a head (2 Kgs 11:17) are folded into the same definition. This is real boundary disagreement within the same category — REFINED, not DIVERGENT, since the central referent (God's binding covenantal bond with His people) remains intact and no consensus claim must be rejected as false of the same referent.
strongest_objection: One could argue this is merely MATCH: the consensus also affirms divine initiation, commanded terms, blood ratification, and law written on the heart, so the book's 'head' language is just vocabulary for what everyone already concedes, and Deut 4:13's equation of covenant with the ten commandments is standard exegesis. Against classifying as REFINED, the objector would say the book's rejection of the 'contract' view targets a straw man the consensus does not actually hold as primary. The rebuttal is that the book's re-identification of covenant as the word itself (not the relationship) and its definitional headship structure genuinely reclassify what the term names and exclude readings (bilateral treaty/contract) that the consensus lists as common.
